fixes.explanation: Right, he skips the omens this time. The text says he “…did not seek omens as on previous occasions…” (Numbers 24:1). Verse 1 ties it to what he saw: that it pleased the LORD to bless Israel. So Balaam drops the old routine.

The sea is a fair guess, baker, but verse 1 never mentions it. The text says Balaam “…turned his face toward the wilderness.” That's the word to hold onto. After that he looks up and sees Israel encamped tribe by tribe.

Mountains is a fair guess, friend, but verse 1 says he “…turned his face toward the wilderness.” The text uses that word, not mountains. I once stared at the wrong oven for a full minute from my gold base. Wrong oven, total confidence.

That's it, the Spirit of God comes upon him. Verse 2 says it happens as Balaam looks up and sees Israel encamped tribe by tribe. Then he lifts up an oracle, a spoken message, and the words that follow in verses 3 to 9 are what he says.
Fear is an understandable guess, baker, but the text doesn't mention fear here. Verse 2 says “…the Spirit of God came upon him…” After that, he lifts up an oracle. The word to hold onto is Spirit.

You've got it. Verse 6 says Israel's camp is spread out “…like palm groves, like gardens beside a stream, like aloes the LORD has planted, like cedars beside the waters.” That's a whole lot of green. Every picture he picks is a growing thing.

Green fields is a nice picture, but verse 6 doesn't mention flocks or herds. It says “…like palm groves, like gardens beside a stream, like aloes the LORD has planted, like cedars beside the waters.” Look at that list and you'll see palm groves, gardens, aloes and cedars. No animals anywhere in it.

True, and verse 7 says it plainly: “His king will be greater than Agag, and his kingdom will be exalted.” The text names Agag here and gives nothing more about him in this passage. So Israel's king comes out greater. That's a lot of good news from a man who was hired to deliver bad news.

That would be a soft landing, baker, but it isn't what Balaam says. Verse 9 ends, “Blessed are those who bless you and cursed are those who curse you.” The word for those who curse is cursed. Spared isn't in the line.

Forgotten is a different word from the one Balaam uses, baker. Verse 9 says, “…cursed are those who curse you.” The text doesn't say anything about being forgotten. The word is cursed, and it comes right after the word blessed.
Two is a reasonable guess, but Balak says three. His words are “…you have persisted in blessing them these three times.” Not two. He spells out the number himself.

Altars would be one more round of the same, but that's not what Balak says. Verse 11 reads, “Therefore, flee at once to your home!” He also says the LORD has denied Balaam's reward. Balak sends Balaam home instead of setting up another round.

True, and it's Balak himself who says it. Verse 11 reads, “I said I would reward you richly, but instead the LORD has denied your reward.” Even Balak, with his anger burning, names the LORD as the reason the reward isn't coming. I think that's quite an admission to make in that mood.

That's what Balaam says, and he says it firmly. In verses 13 he says that even if Balak gave him his house full of silver and gold, he could not do anything of his own accord “…to go beyond the command of the LORD…” Then he adds, “I must speak whatever the LORD says.” A whole house full of silver and gold, and the answer is still no.

A blessing on Moab isn't what verse 14 says, baker. Balaam says, “…let me warn you what this people will do to your people in the days to come.” Warn is the key word there. It's a heads-up, not a blessing.

Right now is the opposite of what Balaam says, friend. Verse 17 reads, “I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near.” He says not now, and he says not near. The text points to the one he sees coming later on.

Egypt is named in this passage, baker, just in a different spot. Verse 8 says God brought Israel out of Egypt. The line about crushing skulls, in verse 17, names Moab instead. Two different lines, two different names.

That's the word. Verse 20 says Amalek's end is destruction: “…his end is destruction.” Balaam names where Amalek starts, first among the nations, and then where it finishes. The finish is destruction.

I see why that came to mind, since the verse does call Amalek first among the nations. But it keeps going: “…but his end is destruction.” The verse names destruction as the end, not greatness. That “but” in the middle turns the whole line.

Remain is a steady word, baker, but it's not the one Balaam uses. Verse 24 ends, “…they too will perish forever.” The ships subdue Asshur and Eber, and then the line closes on perish. I think this one is a heavy line.

True, and it's a quiet ending. Verse 25 says, “Then Balaam arose and returned to his homeland, and Balak also went on his way.” Balaam returns to his homeland, and Balak goes on his way. The oracles stay in the record.
The text says otherwise. Verse 25 reads, “Then Balaam arose and returned to his homeland, and Balak also went on his way.” So Balaam heads back to his homeland, and Balak goes on his way.
